title.en: Purun-pacha: Nations from Beyond Potosi and the Night Demons
title.zh: 普龍帕查:波托西之外的族群與夜間惡魔

region.en: Potosi region, from which the nations came (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 族群所來自的波托西地區(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Salcamayhua, native of Collasuyu, wrote c. 1613; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the age called Purun-pacha all the nations of Ttahuantin-suyu came from beyond Potosi in four or five armies arrayed for war, settling district by district as they advanced. The period lasted a vast number of years. When the country was peopled there was a great want of space: wars and quarrels, fortresses on every side, daily encounters, and no peace. In the middle of the night the people heard the Hapi-ñuños - the demons who in ancient times walked visibly over the land and violently carried off men, women and children - disappearing with mournful complaints, crying out 'We are conquered, we are conquered, alas that we should lose our bands!' Salcamayhua, a Christian, reads this as the demons conquered by Christ on the cross of Calvary; in the native frame it records the silencing of the old night-spirits at the turning of the age.
summary.zh: 在名為「普龍帕查」的時代,大蘇尤(Ttahuantin-suyu)所有族群自波托西之外而來,分四五路列陣遷徙,且行且擇地而居。此期歷時極久。人滿之後,土地不足,戰爭四起,堡壘林立,日日交鋒,永無寧日。夜半之時,人們聽見「哈皮紐紐」——古時顯形於大地、夜裡擄走男女孩童的惡魔——哀號而去:「我們敗了,我們敗了,竟失了我們的隊伍!」基督徒薩爾卡馬瓦將此讀作惡魔在加爾瓦略山上被基督釘十字所敗;而在本源的神話語境中,這是舊夜靈隨時代更替而消音的記錄。

sensitivity.note: Salcamayhua (c. 1613) is the one major Andean-authored colonial narrative; his Christian overlay is quoted as part of the record, not as native belief.

passages.text: They say that, in the time of Purun-pacha, all the nations of Ttahuantin-suyu came from beyond Potosi in four or five armies arrayed for war. They settled in the different districts as they advanced. This period was called Ccallac-pacha or Tutayac-pacha. As each company selected suitable places for their homes and lands, they called this Purunpacharacyaptin. This period lasted for a vast number of years.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: After the country was peopled, there was a great want of space, and, as the land was insufficient, there were wars and quarrels, and all the nations occupied themselves in making fortresses, and every day there were encounters and battles, and there was no rest from these tumults, insomuch that the people never enjoyed any peace. Then, in the middle of the night, they heard the Hapi-ñuños disappearing, with mournful complaints, and crying out: 'We are conquered, we are conquered, alas that we should lose our bands!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: In ancient times, in the days of Purun-pacha, they say that the Hapi-ñuñus walked visibly over all the land, and it was unsafe to go out at night, for they violently carried off men, women, and children, like infernal tyrants and enemies of the human race. By the cry at midnight it must be understood, in Salcamayhua's reading, that the devils were conquered by Jesus Christ our Lord on the cross on Mount Calvary.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim; the Calvary gloss is the author's own.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Tonapa the Bearded Preacher: Staff, Stick of Commandments and Cursed Lakes
title.zh: 鬚髯傳道者托納帕:手杖、誡命之杖與受詛之湖

region.zh: 科利亞蘇尤阿波坦波村(帕卡里坦波)(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Some years after the Hapi-ñuñus had been driven out, there arrived in Ttahuantin-suyu a bearded man of middle height, with long hair and a rather long shirt, somewhat past his prime, grey-haired and lean. He travelled with his staff, teaching the natives with much love, calling them all his sons and daughters, healing the sick by his touch, speaking all languages better than the natives. They called him Tonapa or Tarapaca (an eagle), the servant, the preacher. The people would not listen, thinking little of him. At the village of Apo-tampu - Paccari-tampu - he arrived very tired at a marriage feast; the chief listened kindly, and Tonapa gave him a stick from his own staff, on which each chapter of his precepts was marked and scored: the Caçi-caçi, the commandments of God. But in Yamquesupa he was treated with insolence and driven away, often sleeping in the fields with only his shirt, a mantle and a book; he cursed that village so that it was covered with water - the lake called Yamquisupaloiga. On the high hill Cacha-pucara he burned an idol in the form of a woman, destroying it with the hill; and where a wedding crowd would not hear him, he cursed them and they were turned into stones, seen to this day in Pucara and other places. Salcamayhua asks: was he not the glorious apostle St Thomas?
summary.zh: 哈皮紐紐被逐後數年,一位鬚髯、長髮、身著長衫的中年男子來到大蘇尤:他已過盛年,頭髮灰白,身形清瘦,拄杖而行,滿懷慈愛教導土人,稱眾人皆其兒女;他以手觸身治癒病者,操各種語言比土人還流利。人們稱他為托納帕或塔拉帕卡(意為鷹)、僕人、傳道者。但民眾不聽,輕視他。他疲憊地抵達阿波坦波村(即帕卡里坦波)時,正值婚宴;酋長善意聽道,托納帕便從自己手杖上折下一枝交給他,在杖上刻記誡命各章——即「卡西-卡西」,上帝的誡命。而在亞姆克蘇帕村,他遭辱罵驅逐,常只以長衫、斗篷與一本書露宿野外;他遂咒詛此村,大水將其淹沒,即今亞姆克蘇帕湖。在高山卡查-普卡拉,他焚毀一座女形神像,連山一併毀去。在另一處婚宴上,群眾不聽他講道,他咒詛眾人化為石頭——普卡拉等處至今猶見。薩爾卡馬瓦自問:這位托納帕,豈非榮耀的使徒聖多默?

sensitivity.note: The Tonapa cycle is the classic bearded-culture-hero tradition; Salcamayhua's apostle-Thomas identification is a colonial gloss to be reported, not endorsed. Tagged culture-hero against the cross-tradition cluster.

passages.text: Some years after the devils called Hapi-ñuñus Achacallas had been driven out of the land, there arrived, in these kingdoms of Ttahuantin-suyu, a bearded man, of middle height, with long hair, and in a rather long shirt. They say that he was somewhat past his prime, for he already had grey hairs, and he was lean. He travelled with his staff, teaching the natives with much love, and calling them all his sons and daughters. As he went through all the land, he performed many miracles. The sick were healed by his touch. He spoke all languages better than the natives. They called him Tonapa or Tarapaca (Tarapaca means an eagle) Uiracocharapacha yachipachan or Pachaccan - the servant, and Uicchaycamayoc, a preacher. Although he preached the people did not listen, for they thought little of him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: This man came to the village of a chief called Apo-tampu (this Apo-tampu is Paccari-tampu) very tired, at a time when they were celebrating a marriage feast. His doctrines were listened to by the chief with friendly feelings, but his vassals heard them unwillingly. From that day the wanderer was a guest of Apo-tampu, to whom it is said that he gave a stick from his own staff, and through this Apo-tampu the people listened with attention to the words of the stranger, receiving the stick from his hands. Thus they received what he preached in a stick, marking and scoring on it each chapter of his precepts. The old men used to say that Caçi-caçi were the commandments of God, and especially the seven precepts, with severe punishments for those who broke them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: This worthy, named Thonapa, is said to have visited all the provinces of the Colla-suyu, preaching to the people without cessation, until one day he entered the town of Yamquesupa. There he was treated with great insolence and contempt, and driven away; they say that he often slept in the fields, without other covering than the long shirt he wore, a mantle, and a book. They say that Thonapa cursed that village, so that it was covered with water. The site is now called Yamquisupaloiga; it is a lake, and nearly all the Indians of that time knew that it was once a village and was then a lake.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that, on a very high hill called Cacha-pucara, there was an idol in the form of a woman, and that Tonapa was inspired with a great hatred against it, and afterwards burnt it, and destroyed it with the hill on which it stood; to this day there are signs of that awful miracle. On another occasion he began to preach with loving words in a town where they were holding a great festival and banquet to celebrate a wedding, and they would not listen: for this they were cursed and turned into stones, which may be seen to this day. The same thing happened in Pucara and other places. He is called Tonapa Uiracocha nipacachan; but was he not the glorious apostle St. Thomas?
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim; the St Thomas gloss is the author's own.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Tonapa at Carapucu: The Cross, the Prison, and the Mantle that Sailed
title.zh: 托納帕在卡拉普庫:十字架、囚禁與浮水之氅

region.en: Carapucu, shore of Lake Titicaca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖畔卡拉普庫(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In his wanderings Tonapa came to the mountains of Caravaya, where he erected a very large cross and carried it on his shoulders to the mountain of Carapucu, where he preached in a loud voice and shed tears. A chief's daughter was sprinkled on the head with water, and the Indians, seeing this, understood that he was washing his head; afterwards Tonapa was taken prisoner and shorn near the great lake of Carapucu, condemned to a cruel death. When day broke a very beautiful youth came to him: 'Do not fear; for I come to call you in the name of the matron, who alone watches over you, and who is about to go to the place of rest.' The youth touched the cords binding Tonapa hand and foot; at five in the morning Tonapa entered the lake with him, his mantle bearing him up on the water and serving in the place of a boat. The chiefs were disturbed, for their idol had been thrown down and destroyed: the huaca flew like the wind to a desert place never visited by men, mourning with its head down, until found by an Indian. Tonapa remained a long time on the rock called Titicaca, then passed Tiquina to Chacamarca and came to Tiyahuanacu (Tiahuanaco); the people, drinking and dancing, did not listen to his preaching, and out of pure anger he denounced them: all who were dancing were turned into stones, visible to this day. He followed the course of the river Chacamarca until he came to the sea.
summary.zh: 托納帕行至卡拉瓦亞山區,立起一座巨大十字架,肩負至卡拉普庫山,在那裡高聲講道,並流下淚水。一位酋長之女被他以水灑頭,印第安人見了,還以為他在洗頭;其後托納帕在卡拉普庫大湖附近被擒,剃去鬚髮,被判處極刑。天明時分,一位極俊美的少年前來對他說:「不要害怕;奉守護你的那位主母之名,我來召你——她即將歸於安息之地。」少年以手指觸開縛他手足的繩索。清晨五時,托納帕隨少年步入湖中,他的斗篷浮托其身,權作輕舟。酋長們惶惶不安:他們的神像已被推倒毀壞——那瓦卡如風般飛往荒無人跡之地,垂首哀哭,後為一印第安人尋見。托納帕獲釋後,長久留居名為提提卡卡的岩石上,繼而經提基納至查卡馬爾卡,來到蒂亞瓦納科。城中方在飲宴起舞,不聽他講道;他盛怒之下以當地語言咒詛之:正在起舞的人盡數化為石頭,至今可見。他沿查卡馬爾卡河而行,直至海濱。

sensitivity.note: The rescue-at-dawn and mantle-boat episode gives Tonapa a death-defeat pattern; tagged resurrection for the cluster, interpretively.

passages.text: They further say that this Tonapa, in his wanderings, came to the mountains of Caravaya, where he erected a very large cross, and he carried it on his shoulders to the mountain of Carapucu, where he preached in a loud voice, and shed tears. And they say that a daughter of a chief of that province was sprinkled on the head with water, and the Indians, seeing this, understood that he was washing his head. So, afterwards, Tonapa was taken prisoner and shorn, near the great lake of Carapucu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that, when day broke, when Tonapa was a prisoner, a very beautiful youth came to him, and said: 'Do not fear; for I come to call you in the name of the matron, who alone watches over you, and who is about to go to the place of rest.' So saying, he touched the cords, by which Tonapa was tied hand and foot, with his fingers. There were many guards, for Tonapa had been condemned to a cruel death. But at dawn, being five in the morning, he entered the lake with the youth, his mantle bearing him up on the water and serving in the place of a boat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: On his arrival in the town and province of Carapucu, the chiefs and principal men were disturbed at having seen their idol thrown down and destroyed. They say that this idol flew like the wind to a desert place, which was never visited by men. Here the idol or huaca was mourning and lamenting with its head down; and in this plight it was found by an Indian. Tonapa, after he had been freed from the hands of those savages, remained for a long time on a rock called Titicaca, and afterwards he passed by Tiquina to Chacamarca, where he came to a town called Tiyahuanacu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that the people of that town were engaged in drinking and dancing when Tonapa came to preach to them, and they did not listen to him. Then, out of pure anger, he denounced them in the language of the land; and, when he departed from that place, all the people who were dancing were turned into stones, and they may be seen to this day. Tonapa then followed the course of the river Chacamarca until he came to the sea. This is reported by those most ancient Yncas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Tupac-yauri, the Double Rainbow, and the Speaking Stone of Sañuc
title.zh: 圖帕克-亞烏里、雙虹與薩紐克的開口石

region.en: Sañuc, on the road from Paccari-tampu to Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帕卡里坦波至庫斯科途中的薩紐克(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The staff Tonapa delivered into the hands of Apu-tampu was turned into fine gold on the birth of his son Manco Ccapac Ynca, who had seven brothers and sisters: Ayar-cachi, Ayar-uchu, Ayar-auca and others. Orphaned of Apu Tampu Pacha and Mama Achi, grown to man's estate, Manco Ccapac assembled his people and agreed with his brothers to seek new lands, taking his rich clothes and arms, the golden staff called Tupac-yauri, and two golden cups from which Tonapa had drunk, called Tupac-usi. Marching towards the hill over which the sun rose, he reached the highest point of that land: over Apu Manco Ccapac arose a very beautiful rainbow, and over the rainbow another, so that he seemed to stand in the midst of the rainbows. 'We have a good sign,' he exclaimed; 'we shall have great prosperity and gain many victories.' He descended to Collcapampa singing Chamay huarisca from delight. From Sañuc he saw afar off the form of a man; his youngest brother ran to it, thinking it some Indian, and when he approached the form raised its head: 'It is well that you have come in search of me; for you will find that I am looking for you, and now you are in my power.' The brother stayed; a sister sent to call him stayed too; both nearly died at the huaca of Sañuc. Manco Ccapac went in great wrath and struck the stone on the head with the tupac-yauri. Words came from the midst of the stone as if it was alive: if he had not got that staff, it would also do to him as it pleased. 'Go on,' it added, 'for you have attained to great honour. But these, your brother and sister, have sinned, and it is therefore right that they should be where I am' - meaning the infernal regions; this is called pitusiray sanasiray, one person fastened on the top of another. Manco Ccapac shed tears, returned to the place of the double rainbow, bemoaned his loss - 'the most unfortunate of orphans' - but the rainbow strengthened him and removed his sorrows; thence the place was called Huaynacaptiy.
summary.zh: 托納帕交到阿波坦波手中的那根手杖,在其子曼科·卡帕克出生時化為純金。曼科有兄弟姐妹七人:亞亞爾-卡奇、亞亞爾-烏丘、亞亞爾-奧卡等。父母(阿波坦波帕查與瑪瑪阿奇)亡故後,曼科長成,召集族人,與兄弟們商定另覓新土,帶上華服兵甲、名為「圖帕克-亞烏里」的金杖,以及托納帕飲過的兩只金杯「圖帕克-烏西」。他們朝太陽升起之山而行,登上此地最高之峰:一道彩虹現於曼科頭上,其上又現一道,曼科遂似置身雙虹之間。「此乃吉兆!」他歡呼,「我們必獲大運,多打勝仗。」他唱著《夏馬伊-瓦里斯卡》,欣然下到科爾卡潘帕。在薩紐克,他遠望見一個人影;最小的兄弟以為是個印第安人,跑上前去,那影子卻抬起頭來:「你來尋我,正合我意——我在此等你,如今你已落入我掌中。」兄弟一去不返;遣妹去喚,亦然;二人俱困於薩紐克瓦卡,瀕臨氣絕。曼科大怒親往,掄起金杖猛擊那石頭的頭部。石中竟傳出話語,彷彿活物:「若非你手持此杖,我亦能任意處置你。去吧——你已得大位。但你這兄妹二人有罪,理當與我同處」——意即幽冥之地。此謂「皮圖西拉伊-薩納西拉伊」,一人疊於另一人之頂。曼科見兄妹身陷險境,自然流淚,回到雙虹之地哀慟,自稱「最不幸的孤兒」;然而彩虹為他壯膽,掃盡其憂傷。自此那地方名為「瓦伊納卡普提伊」。

sensitivity.note: Salcamayhua's version of the founder's march, with the Tonapa staff linking the culture-hero to the dynasty; the petrified siblings parallel Sarmiento's Ayar-stone episodes.

passages.text: They say that the staff which Tonapa delivered into the hands of Apu-tampu was turned into fine gold on the birth of his son named Manco Ccapac Ynca, who had seven brothers and sisters. Their names were Ayar-cachi, Ayar-uchu, Ayar-auca, etc. The said Apu Manco Ccapac, after the death of his father and mother, named Apu Tampu Pacha and Mama Achi, being now an orphan, but grown to man's estate, assembled his people to see what power he had to prosecute the new conquests which he meditated. Finding some difficulties, he agreed with his brothers to seek new lands, taking his rich clothes and arms, and the staff which had been left by Tonapa. This staff was called Tupac-yauri. He also had two golden cups from which Tonapa had drunk, called Tupac-usi.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus he set out, with his brothers, towards the hill over which the sun rose. They say that, marching in this direction, he arrived at the hill which was the highest point in that land. Then, over Apu Manco Ccapac arose a very beautiful rainbow, and over the rainbow appeared another, so that Apu Manco Ccapac seemed to be in the midst of the rainbows. He exclaimed: 'We have a good sign. We shall have great prosperity and gain many victories, and we shall obtain all that we desire.' After saying this, he joyfully advanced, singing the song of Chamay huarisca from mere delight. Then he descended to Collcapampa with his brothers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the town of Sañuc he saw, afar off, the form of a man. One of his brothers ran towards it, thinking that it was some Indian; but when he came up to it, he saw one like an Indian, looking most fierce and cruel with bloodshot eyes. When he approached, the form raised its head, and said: 'It is well that you have come in search of me; for you will find that I am looking for you, and now you are in my power.' Manco Ccapac, seeing that his brother was so long in returning, sent one of his sisters to call him. But she also remained away, and both were kept at the huaca of Sañuc. Manco Ccapac went himself in great wrath, and found them both nearly dead. He asked them why they stayed away so long, and they answered by complaining of a stone which was between the two.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Apu Manco Ccapac struck the stone or huaca with much fury, giving it blows with his tupac-yauri on the head. Then words came from the midst of the stone, as if it was alive, saying, that if he had not got that staff, it would also do to him as it pleased. 'Go on,' it added; 'for you have attained to great honour. But these, your brother and sister, have sinned, and it is therefore right that they should be where I am,' meaning the infernal regions. This is called pitusiray sanasiray, which means one person fastened on the top of another. Manco Ccapac shed tears of natural grief and sorrow, and went back to the place where he had first seen the rainbow. He bemoaned the loss of his brother and sister, and exclaimed that he was the most unfortunate of orphans. But the rainbow strengthened him, and removed all his sorrows and afflictions; from that time the place was called Huaynacaptiy.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Hurin-cancha and Hanan-cancha: The Founding of Cuzco
title.zh: 下泉與上泉:庫斯科之奠基

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: From Collcapampa Manco Ccapac went with the tupac-yauri in his hand, with a sister named Ypa Mama Huaco, and with another sister and a brother; they came to Huamantiana, where they remained some time, and thence marched to Coricancha, where they found a place suitable for a settlement. There was good water from Hurin-chacan and Hanan-chacan - whence the names of Hurin-Cuzco and Hanan-Cuzco - two springs. A rock was called by the natives by the name of Cuzco-cara-urumi, whence the place came to be called Cuzco-pampa and Cuzco-llacta, and the Yncas afterwards Cuzco-Ccapac and Cuzco-Ynca. This Ynca Apu Manco Ccapac married one of his own sisters named Mama Ocllo, and this marriage was celebrated that they might have no equal, and that they might not lose the caste. Then they began to enact good laws for the government of their people, conquering many provinces and nations of those that were disobedient; the tidings of a new Ynca spread widely: some were joyful, others afflicted, when they heard that the Ynca was the most powerful chief, the most valiant, and the most fortunate in arms.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克手持圖帕克-亞烏里金杖,與妹妹伊帕·瑪瑪·瓦科及另一位兄妹,自科爾卡潘帕前往瓦曼蒂亞納,居留有時,再進至科里坎查,見一處宜於建城之地。此地有兩眼好泉,一為烏林-查坎,一為哈南-查坎——烏林庫斯科與哈南庫斯科之名即由此而來。當地人稱此地岩石為「庫斯科-卡拉-烏魯米」,故此地得名庫斯科潘帕、庫斯科利亞克塔;印加王族後亦稱庫斯科-卡帕克、庫斯科-印加。曼科·卡帕克娶其妹瑪瑪·奧克略為妻,此婚所以舉行者,為使二人無與匹敵、血統不致旁落。其後頒良法以治其民,征服諸多不從之邦。新印加之名傳遍四方:聞其為至強至勇、用兵常勝之主,有人歡喜,有人憂懼。

sensitivity.note: Founding with the sibling marriage justifying caste endogamy; tagged divine-marriage for the cluster.

passages.text: Thence he went to Collcapampa with the tupac-yauri in his hand, and with a sister named Ypa mama huaco, and with another sister and a brother. They arrived at Collcapampa, where they were for some days. Thence they went to Huamantiana, where they remained some time, and thence they marched to Coricancha, where they found a place suitable for a settlement. There was good water from Hurinchacan and Hananchacan (whence the names of Hurin-Cuzco and Hanan-Cuzco), which are two springs.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: A rock was called by the natives (who are the Allcayriesas, the Cullinchinas, and the Cayaucachis) by the name of Cuzco-cara-urumi, whence the place came to be called Cuzco-pampa and Cuzco-llacta; and the Yncas were afterwards called Cuzco-Ccapac and Cuzco-Ynca. This Ynca Apu Manco Ccapac married one of his own sisters named Mama Ocllo, and this marriage was celebrated that they might have no equal, and that they might not lose the caste.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they began to enact good laws for the government of their people, conquering many provinces and nations of those that were disobedient. The Ttahuantin-suyus came with a good grace and with rich presents. The tidings of a new Ynca had spread widely. Some were joyful, others were afflicted; when they heard that the Ynca was the most powerful chief, the most valiant, and the most fortunate in arms, that his captains and men of valour were better armed than other men, and that all his affairs were prosperous.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

title.en: The Golden Plate, the Three Windows, and the Trees with Golden Fruit
title.zh: 金板、三窗與結金果之樹

region.zh: 庫斯科科里坎查(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: This Ynca ordered the smiths to make a flat plate of fine gold, which signified that there was a Creator of heaven and earth, and caused it to be fixed in a great house called Ccuricancha pachayachachipac huasin - the house of the teacher of the world. Manco Ccapac was an enemy to the huacas, and as such he destroyed the Curaca Pinao Ccapac with all his idols, and conquered Tocay Ccapac, a great idolater. At the place of his birth he ordered works executed: a masonry wall with three windows, emblems of the house of his fathers whence he descended - the first window called Tampu-toco, the second Maras-toco, the third Sutic-toco, referring to his uncles and grandparents. Two trees typified his father and mother Apu-tampu and Apachamama-achi; he ordered them adorned with roots of gold and silver and with golden fruit; they were called Cceurichachac collquechachac tampu-yracan, for the two trees typified the parents, and the Yncas proceeded from them like fruit from the trees, the trees being as the roots and stems of the Yncas. Later, Huascar Ynca removed the plate of the Creator and substituted another round plate like the sun with rays; yet images of sun and moon stood on either side.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克命金匠打製一塊純金薄板,以誌天地有一造物主,懸於大屋「科里坎查-帕查亞查奇帕克-瓦辛」(即「教世者之屋」)內。曼科敵視瓦卡,毀庫拉卡皮尼亞奧-卡帕克及其一切偶像,又征服大拜偶像者托卡伊-卡帕克。他還在其誕生之地營建工程:一道三窗石牆,象徵其祖居之屋——第一窗名「坦普-托科」,第二窗名「馬拉斯-托科」,第三窗名「蘇蒂克-托科」,分指其叔伯與祖父母。又有兩樹象徵其父母阿波坦波與瑪瑪阿奇;他命人飾以金銀之根、結以金果,稱之為「庫里查查克-科爾克查查克-坦普-伊拉坎」:兩樹喻雙親,印加出自二樹,如樹之結實;二樹即印加之根與幹。後來瓦伊納·卡帕克之後,瓦伊斯卡爾移去造物主金板,代之以日形放射之圓板,而日月之像仍列於兩側。

sensitivity.note: The famous Salcamayhua plate diagram: a Creator-emblem predating the solar cult substitution under Huascar - central to debates on Andean monotheism. Reported as the source has it.

passages.text: This Ynca ordered the smiths to make a flat plate of fine gold; which signified that there was a Creator of heaven and earth; and it was of this shape. He caused it to be fixed in a great house called Ccuricancha pachaya-chachipac huasin. This Ynca Manco Ccapac was an enemy to the huacas, and, as such, he destroyed the Curaca Pinao Ccapac with all his idols. He also conquered Tocay Ccapac, a great idolater.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards he ordered works to be executed at the place of his birth; consisting of a masonry wall with three windows, which were emblems of the house of his fathers whence he descended. The first window was called Tampu-toco, the second Maras-toco, and the third Sutic-toco: referring to his uncles and paternal and maternal grandparents. These two trees typified his father and mother Apu-tampu and Apachamama-achi, and he ordered that they should be adorned with roots of gold and silver, and with golden fruit. Hence they were called Cceurichachac collquechachac tampu-yracan, which means that the two trees typified the parents, and that the Yncas proceeded from them, like fruit from the trees, and that the two trees were as the roots and stems of the Yncas. All these things were executed to record their greatness.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Although Huascar Ynca had placed an image of the sun in the place where that of the Creator had been, yet it shall not be omitted here; for there was an image of the sun and moon on either side of it. They say that a Spaniard gambled for this plate of gold in Cuzco, as Salcamayhua mentions in its place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Pacarisca: Every Tribe Chooses the Place of Its Origin
title.zh: 帕卡里斯卡:各族自擇發源之地

region.zh: 大蘇尤(象徵性標記:庫斯科地區)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Manco Ccapac ordered that the dresses of each village should be different, that the people might be known, for down to this time there were no means of knowing to what village or tribe an Indian belonged. He also ordered, with a view to each tribe being clearly distinguished, that they should choose whence they were descended and from whence they came: as the Indians were very dull and stupid, some chose for their pacarisca or pacarimusca a lake, others a spring, others a rock, others the hills or ravines; but every lineage selected some object for its pacarisca. The hapi-ñuñus deceived those stupid people with little difficulty, entering into the false pacariscas and thence uttering deceitful promises. Every day these pacariscas continued to increase, the origin or pacarinim being the Pacari-tampu. The leading cause of the invention of the pacarinim was that the Ynca Manco Ccapac was often at a loss to know to what village an Indian belonged. He also ordered the heads of infants to be pressed, that they might grow up without audacity and disobedience.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克命各村服飾各異,以便辨識——此前無從得知一印第安人屬何村何族。他又命各族自明其所自出、所從來:印第安人多愚魯,故或擇湖、或擇泉、或擇石、或擇丘陵溝壑為其「帕卡里斯卡」(發源之物),凡世系皆擇一物以奉之。哈皮紐紐惡魔極易欺哄愚民,潛入偽帕卡里斯卡,從中發出欺人之諾。帕卡里斯卡日漸增多,而其總源即「帕卡里坦波」。各州各族皆言:「帕卡里斯坎奇克,烏克斯坎奇克,烏馬昆,奇克帕-帕卡里斯坎。」立帕卡里尼姆(發源之制)之主因,乃印加王常難辨某印第安人屬於何村。曼科又命壓嬰兒之頭,使其長成後不致狂妄不遜。

sensitivity.note: The institutionalization of lineage origin-cults; Salcamayhua's contemptuous framing of commoners ('dull and stupid') is quoted critically.

passages.text: He ordered that the dresses of each village should be different, that the people might be known, for down to this time there were no means of knowing to what village or tribe an Indian belonged. He also ordered, with a view to each tribe being clearly distinguished, that they should choose whence they were descended and from whence they came, and, as the Indians generally were very dull and stupid, some chose, for their pacarisca or pacarimusca, a lake, others a spring, others a rock, others the hills or ravines; but every lineage selected some object for its pacarisca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The devils, or hapi-ñuñus, deceived those stupid people with little difficulty, entering into the false pacariscas, and thence uttering deceitful promises. Every day these pacariscas continued to increase, the origin or pacarinim being the Pacari-tampu. All the provinces and tribes said: Pacariscanchic huccsiscanchic umachun chicpa-pacariscan. The leading cause of the invention of the pacarinim was that the Ynca Manco Ccapac was often at a loss to know to what village an Indian belonged. This Ynca also ordered the heads of infants to be pressed, that they might grow up foolish and without energy; for he thought that Indians with large round heads, being audacious in any enterprise, might also be disobedient.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Apachitas: The Stone Heaps and the Thrower of Coca
title.zh: 阿帕奇塔斯:石堆與投古柯之俗

region.en: Ravines between Chacamarca and Angaraes (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 查卡馬爾卡至安加拉斯之間的溝壑(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Sinchi Ruca Ynca, who began to rule over all the territory of his father, was a great patron of agriculture, of weaving cloth and of mining, but seldom went abroad; when he desired to make conquests he sent his captains and their men. In each ravine they had to take stones to make usnus, certain stones arranged in heaps. They say that an Indian wizard appeared to one of the officers of war, and told him that the heaps must be called apachitas. A rite was established, that every passer by should bring a great stone; and the wizard also told the officer of the Ynca that all the soldiers must throw their coca pallets on the heap as they passed, saying: 'Saycoyñiycaypitac quipasiyon coyñiypashinatac.' From that time they began to bring stones and to throw coca, because the wizard had so ordered it.
summary.zh: 辛奇·羅卡·印加繼承父土,重農桑、織布、開礦,而少親征;欲征伐則遣將領兵。每逢溝壑,軍中須取石壘成「烏斯努」(成堆之石)。相傳一位印第安巫師顯現於某軍官之前,告知此堆當名為「阿帕奇塔斯」;並立一俗:凡過者皆須取一大石投之;巫師又囑軍官,眾兵過堆時須將古柯葉投於堆上,口誦:「賽科伊尼伊卡伊皮塔克,基帕西永,科伊尼亞希納塔克。」自此人人運石投古柯,皆因巫師之命。

sensitivity.note: Etiology of the apachita road-shrines still visible along Andean trails.

passages.text: Sinchi Ruca Ynca began to rule over all the territory of his father, and was a great patron of agriculture, of weaving cloth, and of mining. He was not much addicted to warlike affairs, for, being a very proud man, and of haughty disposition, he seldom went abroad. When he desired to make conquests he sent his captains and their men. In each ravine they had to take stones to make usnus, which are certain stones arranged in heaps.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that an Indian wizard appeared to one of the officers of war, and told him that the heaps must be called apachitas. A rite was established, which was that every passer by should bring a great stone; and the wizard also told the officer of the Ynca that all the soldiers must throw their coca pallets on the heap as they passed, saying: Saycoyñiycaypitac quipasiyon coyñiypashinatac. From that time they began to bring stones and to throw coca, because the wizard had so ordered it.

title.en: The Silent Altar: Manco Capac's Last Prayer and the Head of His Son
title.zh: 沉默的祭壇:曼科·卡帕克末年祈禱與親子之血

region.zh: 庫斯科科里坎查(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When the Ynca Manco Ccapac was very old, he went down on his knees and prayed for the prosperity of his son in a long Quechua prayer, recalling the sun, moon and day, the silence of night and the light of dawn; after this he always remembered Tonapa in a second prayer. Having said this he watched to see if he might have a sign from the Creator. He offered a very white lamb upon an altar, a sacrifice called arpay. When no answer was given, he ordered the most beautiful of his sons, aged about eight years, to be offered up, cutting off his head, and sprinkling the blood over the fire, that the smoke might reach the Maker of heaven and earth. To all these offerings no answer was ever given in Coricancha.
summary.zh: 曼科·卡帕克年邁之際,跪而為其子祈福,以克丘亞語誦長禱,提及日月與晝、黑夜之靜與黎明之光;繼而常念托納帕,另誦一禱。禱畢,他守望求造物主賜一徵兆。他在祭壇上獻一極白之羔,此祭名為「阿爾帕伊」。無有應答,他便下令獻上自己最美的、年約八歲的兒子:斷其首,以血灑火,使煙上達天地之造主。然而在科里坎查,這一切祭獻始終未獲一答。

sensitivity.note: A stark episode of dynastic child sacrifice framed as unanswered prayer; Salcamayhua's religious melancholy is quoted as given.

passages.text: They say that when the Ynca Manco Ccapac was very old, he went down on his knees, and prayed for the prosperity of his son in these words: 'A Uiracochantic çicapac caycaricachun cay raimicachun ñeca apa hinamtima chiccha camac maypin canqui...' (a long Quechua petition recalling sun, moon, day, night and dawn). After this he always remembered Tonapa, saying: 'Runa rallcapacpalhacan yananssi cahuac...' - a second prayer, calling Tonapa by name.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim; Quechua prayers quoted in the translation's transcription.

When no answer was given, he ordered the most beautiful of his sons, aged about eight years, to be offered up, cutting off his head, and sprinkling the blood over the fire, that the smoke might reach the Maker of heaven and earth. To all these offerings no answer was ever given in Coricancha.
